s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Demonstrative or Deictic Reference
s.d: a reference to an entity regarded as a part of the discourse setting,{N:001} with pejorative meaning in certain contexts{N:002}
a marker of an explanation or a clarification in the same or a different language

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the Aramaic name of a Christian woman in Joppa whose name was interpreted as {L:Δορκάς<SDBG:Δορκάς:000000>} ({D:93.101})

s.dp: Arrange, Organize › Organize [of events and states]
s.d: a proper and correct order
s.g: right order; good order; in order; in an orderly manner

s.d: pertaining to that which has been decided upon in advance

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.d: to be sorrowful and complain, presumably on the basis of wretched circumstances

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: hardship resulting in wretchedness
s.c: ‘Wretchedness’ may be expressed idiomatically in some languages as ‘to have nothing’ or ‘to have even one’s shirt in rags.’

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: pertaining to being in a wretched state, either mentally or physically

s.dp: Weight › Pound, Talent [Specific Units of Weight]
s.d: pertaining to weighing a talent or 125 Roman pounds of twelve ounces each or approximately ninety pounds (English weight) or forty kilograms
s.c: It may, however, be better to use in ⟦Revelation 16:21|Revelation 16:21⟧ an expression with a more general sense, for example, ‘great stones of hail weighing almost a hundred pounds’ or ‘… forty kilos.’

s.d: a Greek monetary unit (also a unit of weight) with a value which fluctuated, depending upon the particular monetary system which prevailed at a particular period of time (a silver talent was worth approximately six thousand denarii with gold talents worth at least thirty times that much)
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 25:15|Matthew 25:15⟧ what is important is the relative number of talents or sums of money. In a number of translations the respective amounts are stated in terms of local currency. For example, in English one may speak of five thousand dollars as equivalent to five talents, though in terms of buying power, five talents would be worth much more than five thousand dollars. What is important, however, in this story is not the precise sums of money but the relative amount which was given to the different servants.|The ‘ten thousand talents’ referred to in ⟦Matthew 18:24|Matthew 18:24⟧ would be equivalent to millions of denarii. The sum in this parable is perhaps greatly exaggerated, precisely in order to emphasize the vast differences between the two debts. It is also true, of course, that in ancient times persons with extensive mercantile businesses sometimes became slaves as a result of defeat in war, and they were purchased by business syndicates together with their business enterprises, which they would continue to manage.

s.dp: People › Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern
s.d: (an Aramaic word in an emphatic form) the designation for a little girl, probably implying affectionate concern

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a room in the interior of a house, normally without windows opening to the outside
s.c: In ⟦Luke 12:3|Luke 12:3⟧ the emphasis is upon the strictly private location of the inner room. In such a context one may translate ‘a strictly private room’ or ‘a small room in the center of the house.’

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a room for the storage of valuables
s.c: ταμεῖον and θησαυρός may often be rendered by descriptive phrases, for example, ‘a room where valuable things are kept’ or ‘a place where valuables are stored.’|In ⟦Matthew 12:35|Matthew 12:35⟧ θησαυρός is used figuratively (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ ἐκβάλλει ἀγαθά ‘a good man draws good things from his good storehouse,’ meaning ‘… storehouse of good things’) to describe the heart as a kind of storehouse or treasure.

s.d: an ordered or arranged sequence

s.dp: Arrange, Organize › Organize [of events and states]
s.d: a proper and correct order
s.g: right order; good order; in order; in an orderly manner
s.c: In ⟦Colossians 2:5|Colossians 2:5⟧ τάξις may refer to the orderly manner in which the church at Colossae conducted its affairs or carried on its worship.

s.d: kind or type of entity, implying a contrast-comparison to other similar entities
s.c: It is possible that τάξις in ⟦Hebrews 5:6|Hebrews 5:6⟧ refers to a kind of priest on the basis of being in a particular grouping or order of priests, but there seems to be no reference to any higher rank or position.

s.d: (compare ταπεινός[c] ‘of low status,’ {D:87.61}) pertaining to being discouraged and lacking in hope, with the possible implication of some association with low social status

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Humility
s.d: pertaining to being unpretentious in one’s behavior
s.c: In some languages the expression ‘humble in spirit’ or ‘humble in heart’ may be expressed as ‘speaking only soft words’ or ‘without shouting at others.’

s.dp: Status › Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
s.d: pertaining to having low and humble status

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Gentleness, Mildness
s.d: pertaining to being meek, with the implication of low status

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Humility
s.d: the quality of humility
s.c: The rendering of ταπεινοφροσύνη in ⟦Colossians 2:18|Colossians 2:18⟧ as ‘false humility’ is justified in terms of the context, but there is nothing in the word ταπεινοφροσύνη itself which means ‘false.’ It would be possible to render ταπεινοφροσύνη in ⟦Colossians 2:18|Colossians 2:18⟧ as ‘subjection to,’ and one might render the entire expression as ‘in abject worship of angels.’ In other languages ‘false humility’ may be rendered as ‘just pretending to be humble’ or ‘appearing to be humble but really being proud.’

s.d: to cause something to become low in height
s.c: For another (probably preferred) interpretation of ⟦Luke 3:5|Luke 3:5⟧, see LN 79.87.

s.d: to cause something to become level
s.g: to level off; to make level
s.c: One might argue that ταπεινόω in ⟦Luke 3:5|Luke 3:5⟧ is to be understood as ‘to be brought low,’ but in contrast with πληρωθήσεται, which refers to filling up valleys, ταπεινωθήσεται should perhaps be understood as referring to ‘leveling off’ mountains and hills. For this other interpretation of ταπεινόω in ⟦Luke 3:5|Luke 3:5⟧, see LN 81.7.

s.dp: Status › Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
s.d: to cause someone to be in a low status
s.g: to make humble; to bring down low

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Humility
s.d: (derivative of {L:ταπεινός<SDBG:ταπεινός:000001>}[b] ‘humble,’ {D:88.52}) to cause someone to be or to become humble
s.c: A strictly literal rendering of ‘he who humbles himself’ could be misunderstood as ‘one who despises himself’ or ‘one who has no regard for himself.’ In the context of ⟦Matthew 18:4|Matthew 18:4⟧ it is often important to use an idiomatic expression which will adequately convey the meaning, for example, ‘one who causes his heart to bow down’ or even ‘one who makes his heart small.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Shame, Disgrace, Humiliation
s.d: to cause someone to become disgraced and humiliated, with the implication of embarrassment and shame
s.g: to humiliate; to put to shame

s.dp: Status › Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
s.d: to live in circumstances regarded as characteristic of low status
s.g: to live in humble circumstances; to live like those of low status
s.c: In a number of languages ταπεινόομαι in ⟦Philippians 4:12|Philippians 4:12⟧ may be rendered as ‘to live like poor people.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Humility
s.d: the quality of unpretentious behavior, suggesting a total lack of arrogance or pride
s.c: In some languages humility is expressed indirectly by an idiomatic phrase, for example, ‘to live without strutting’ or ‘to walk without wanting to be noticed.’

s.dp: Status › Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
s.d: the state of low status, with the probable implication of humility
to cause movement, usually as the result of shaking or stirring
s.g: to cause to move; to stir up
s.c: This word is found as a variant reading only: ἄγγελος γὰρ κυρίου κατὰ καιρὸν κατέβαινεν ἐν τῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ καὶ ἐταράσσετο τὸ ὕδωρ ‘from time to time an angel of the Lord would come down in the pool and cause the water to move’ ⟦John 5:4|John 5:4⟧ (apparatus).

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ταράσσω<SDBG:ταράσσω:000000>}[a] ‘to stir up,’ {D:16.3}) to cause acute emotional distress or turbulence
to cause people to riot against
s.g: to stir up against; to start a riot; to cause an uproar

s.d: a serious disturbance

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Worry, Anxiety, Distress, Peace
s.d: a state of acute distress and great anxiety, with the additional possible implications of dismay and confusion
s.c: Since τάραχος refers to the type of extreme anxiety which borders on fear, it may be possible in some languages to use a double expression, ‘were greatly distressed and afraid.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Ταρσός<SDBG:Ταρσός:000000>} ‘Tarsus,’ {D:93.596}) a person who lives in or is a native of Tarsus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the capital of Cilicia in southeast Asia Minor

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
s.d: (derivative of τάρταρος ‘Tartarus,’ ‘hell,’ as a place of torture or torment, not occurring in the NT) to cast into or to cause to remain in Tartarus
s.g: to hold in Tartarus; to cast into hell
s.c: In many cases it is confusing to add still another term for a designation of hell by transliterating the Greek τάρταρος, and so most translators have preferred to render ταρταρόω as either ‘to cast into hell’ or ‘to keep in hell,’ thus using for ‘hell’ the same term as is employed for a rendering of the Greek term γέεννα (LN 1.21).

s.dp: Control, Rule › Assign to a Role or Function
s.d: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
s.g: to appoint; to designate; to assign; to give a task to
s.c: Though τάσσω in ⟦Acts 13:48|Acts 13:48⟧ has sometimes been interpreted as meaning ‘to choose,’ there seems to be far more involved than merely a matter of selection, since a relationship is specifically assigned.

s.d: to cause someone to be in a state involving an order or arrangement
s.g: to cause to be; to be placed

s.d: to give detailed instructions as to what must be done{N:001}
s.g: to order; to instruct; to tell; to command

s.d: to propose something to someone
s.c: It is also possible to understand τάσσω in ⟦Acts 28:23|Acts 28:23⟧ as meaning ‘to arrange,’ but in ⟦Acts 28:23|Acts 28:23⟧ it would seem that τάσσω implies not only proposing a date but obtaining an agreement.

s.d: to do something with devotion, with the possible implication of systematic, regular activity
s.g: to do with devotion; to give oneself to

s.d: male bovine; large ruminant animal with horns and cloven hoofs; used for sacrifice and for meat, as a beast of burden, or for pulling a cart or a plow
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘bull’ is simply a generic term for cattle to which is added a specific designation such as ‘male.’

s.d: a place for burying
s.c: It is also possible to understand ταφή in the context of ⟦Matthew 27:7|Matthew 27:7⟧ as a reference to the process of burial, and one may therefore translate ⟦Matthew 27:7|Matthew 27:7⟧ as ‘they used the money to buy the Potter’s Field to bury foreigners.’

s.d: a construction for the burial of the dead; often a natural cave or hewn out of bedrock{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between a grave (a hole in the ground in which a corpse is placed) and a tomb (a construction built above the surface of the ground for housing a corpse). In some contexts, however, it may be better to use a more generic expression, for example, ‘places where people are buried’ or ‘places where corpses are placed.’ In ⟦Mark 5:2|Mark 5:2⟧ it is important to avoid a term which would designate merely graves, for the demoniac who met Jesus was not living down in graves in the ground, but had found some habitation either in burial caves or in tombs constructed above ground.

s.d: pertaining to a low probability of occurrence

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a very short extent of time
s.c: In ⟦Galatians 1:6|Galatians 1:6⟧ ταχέως refers clearly to the relatively brief period of time before the Galatians abandoned their earlier convictions.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a very short extent of time
s.c: In ⟦2 Peter 2:1|2 Peter 2:1⟧ ταχινός may refer to the swift nature of the destruction or to the fact that destruction comes after a relatively brief period of time.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: a very brief period of time
s.g: a very short while; quickly (in combination with the preposition ἐν)
s.c: In ⟦Acts 22:18|Acts 22:18⟧ τάχος evidently refers to a brief period of time before fulfilling the admonition to leave Jerusalem.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a very short extent of time
s.c: In ⟦John 11:29|John 11:29⟧ ταχύ probably refers to the short period of time between Mary‘s hearing about Jesus and her getting up to go out to meet him. It is, of course, also possible to interpret ταχύ in ⟦John 11:29|John 11:29⟧ as referring to the rapidity of Mary‘s movement in getting up and going out to meet Jesus.|Again, in ⟦John 13:27|John 13:27⟧ the emphasis is upon the brief period of time before Judas is to do what he had set out to do.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time
a marker of a close relationship between coordinate, nonsequential items
a marker of a close relationship between sequential events or states
a marker of a totality of two closely related elements
a marker of a totality of two closely related elements
a marker of a closely related coordinate set
s.g: as … so; not only … but also

s.d: a particularly strong permanent wall, primarily the wall built around a city for its protection
s.c: In a number of languages a translator must make a clear distinction between a wall of a house and a city wall. The wall of a house may be called ‘a side of a house’ and an inner wall ‘a partition in a house,’ while a city wall is often related to terms such as ‘barricade’ or ‘fence.’ Hence, a city wall may be called ‘a fortified fence around a city.’

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: that which causes something to be known as verified or confirmed
s.c: In a number of languages ‘convincing proof’ is rendered as ‘that which causes one to know for sure’ or ‘… with certainty.’

s.dp: People › Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern
s.d: (extension of meaning of {L:τέκνον<SDBG:τέκνον:000000>}[a] ‘child, offspring,’ {D:10.36}) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
s.g: my child; my dear friend; my dear man; my dear one; my dear lad
s.c: It may be impossible to translate τεκνία literally as ‘my children’ in ⟦1 John 3:7|1 John 3:7⟧ since this might suggest a kinship relationship between the author of 1 John and the people to whom he is addressing his letter. A more satisfactory equivalent in some languages is often ‘my dear friends’ or ‘my dear ones.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: to give birth to a child{N:001}
s.c: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: to give birth to a child{N:001}
s.c: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: one’s immediate offspring, but without specific reference to sex or age
s.c: In languages in which there is no generic term for ‘child’ or ‘offspring,’ one may use ‘son’ or ‘daughter’ or ‘son and daughter,’ singular or plural, depending upon the context.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: successive following generations of those who are biologically related to a reference person
s.c: In the case of γενεά, τέκνον, and σπέρμα (LN 10.29), the reference is not to one’s immediate descendants or offspring (that is to say, to one’s sons or daughters) but to a successive series of such persons, one’s descendants. In some languages such descendants may be called merely ‘the children of one’s children,’ and in other languages one may refer to descendants as ‘those who follow one’ or ‘those who come later.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of τέκνον[a] ‘child,’ {D:10.36}) inhabitants of a particular place
s.c: Only rarely can one preserve the figurative significance of τέκνον as a designation of the inhabitants of an area. Readers are too likely to understand such a reference as applicable only to children who live in a particular place. Even the use of a simile does not assist appreciably, since it would be interpreted as likening the inhabitants of an area to children, probably in the sense of their being immature or incapable. For example, the expression the people of Jerusalem like children would probably lead to serious misunderstanding.

s.dp: People › Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern
s.d: (extension of meaning of τέκνον[a] ‘child, offspring,’ {D:10.36}) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
s.g: my child; my dear friend; my dear man; my dear one; my dear lad
s.c: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate τέκνον in ⟦Matthew 9:2|Matthew 9:2⟧ as ‘child,’ since this might immediately suggest that Jesus was declaring himself to be the father of this man. Furthermore, the paralytic was evidently an adult male. A more satisfactory equivalent would be ‘my dear man’ or ‘my dear fellow.’

s.dp: Guide, Discipline, Follow › Follow, Be a Disciple
s.d: a person who looks to another as being, so to speak, a father in the faith and thus becomes a disciple of that person
s.c: It is also possible that τέκνον in ⟦3 John 1:4|3 John 1:4⟧ is to be understood simply as an affectionate way of talking about persons who in one way or another are in a dependent relationship to someone (see LN 9.46).

s.d: a kind or class of persons, with the implication of possessing certain derived characteristics
s.g: son of; offspring of; child of; kind of; one who has the characteristics of; person of

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: (an idiom, literally: children of light) persons to whom the truth of God has been revealed and who are presumably living according to such truth. See also {D:9.4} and {D:12.15}
s.g: sons of the light; children of the light; people of God
s.c: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘light’ in the metaphorical sense of the truth that comes from God. Such truth is not to be equated with knowledge, but with the principles and practices of right moral behavior. Because of these difficulties in speaking of ‘truth’ as ‘light,’ a number of translators have preferred to use the expression ‘people of God’ for the phrases υἱοὶ τοῦ φωτός, υἱοὶ τῆς ἡμέρας, and τέκνα φωτός. In some instances, however, it is possible to employ ‘light,’ if this is described as ‘light that comes from God’ or even ‘the true light from God.’

s.dp: Help, Care For › Rear, Bring Up
s.d: to raise a child to maturity by providing for physical and psychological needs{N:001}
s.g: to raise; to rear; to bring up
s.c: To raise or bring up children may be expressed in a number of different ways, for example, ‘to give food to children,’ ‘to take care of children,’ ‘to be a parent to children,’ ‘to cause a child to become an adult,’ or ‘to make a child become like oneself.’

s.d: one who uses various materials (wood, stone, and metal) in building
s.c: There is every reason to believe that in biblical times one who was regarded as a τέκτων would be skilled in the use of wood and stone and possibly even metal.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Perfect, Perfection
s.d: pertaining to being perfect in the sense of not lacking any moral quality
s.c: Compare the meaning of τέλειος mature in LN 88.100.

s.d: pertaining to being truly and completely genuine
pertaining to having no defect whatsoever
pertaining to that which is fully accomplished or finished

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Mature Behavior
s.d: pertaining to being mature in one’s behavior
s.c: It is also possible to interpret τέλειος in ⟦Ephesians 4:13|Ephesians 4:13⟧ as meaning ‘perfect’ (see LN 88.36).|In ⟦Matthew 5:48|Matthew 5:48⟧ it is possible that τέλειος also means maturity of behavior, but it is usually interpreted as ‘being perfect,’ since the comparison is made with God (see LN 88.36).

s.d: pertaining to an adult human being
s.c: Though in ⟦Hebrews 5:14|Hebrews 5:14⟧ τέλειος is to be understood in a literal sense, the context as a whole is figurative.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: one who is initiated into a religious community of faith (a meaning which reflects the occurrence of τέλειος as a technical term for persons initiated into the mystery religions)
s.c: In a number of languages ‘initiated’ (⟦Philippians 3:15|Philippians 3:15⟧, ⟦Colossians 1:28|Colossians 1:28⟧) may be best expressed as ‘to become a member of’ or ‘to become a believer in.’ It is possible, however, to interpret τέλειος in ⟦Philippians 3:15|Philippians 3:15⟧ and ⟦Colossians 1:28|Colossians 1:28⟧ as mature spirituality or a state of being spiritually mature (see LN 88.100).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Mature Behavior
s.d: maturity in thought and behavior

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Perfect, Perfection
s.d: a state of perfection, implying some process of maturity

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Perfect, Perfection
s.d: to make perfect in the moral sense
s.g: to make perfect; to perfect; causing perfection
s.c: For another interpretation of τελειόω in ⟦1 John 2:5|1 John 2:5⟧, see LN 73.7.

s.d: to cause to be truly and completely genuine
s.g: to make genuine; to make true; to make completely real
s.c: For another interpretation of τελειόω in ⟦1 John 2:5|1 John 2:5⟧, see LN 88.38.

s.d: to bring an activity to a successful finish{N:001}
s.g: to complete; to finish; to end; to accomplish

s.d: to be completely successful in accomplishing some goal or attaining some state
s.g: to be completely successful; to succeed fully
s.c: For another interpretation of τελειόω in ⟦Philippians 3:12|Philippians 3:12⟧, see LN 53.50.

s.d: to admit into or initiate into faith (possibly based on technical usage in the mystery religions)
s.c: It is important that in ⟦Philippians 3:12|Philippians 3:12⟧ τελειόω is to be understood in the sense of a functional stage of religious attainment: ‘I have already become an initiate.’ For another interpretation of τελειόω in ⟦Philippians 3:12|Philippians 3:12⟧, see LN 68.31.

s.d: to cause to happen for some end result
s.g: to make happen; to fulfill; to bring to fruition; to accomplish; fulfillment

s.d: to attain a state as a goal
a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Perfect, Perfection
s.d: to make perfect in the moral sense
s.g: to make perfect; to perfect; causing perfection

s.d: to cause to happen for some end result
s.g: to make happen; to fulfill; to bring to fruition; to accomplish; fulfillment

s.d: one who makes possible the successful completion of something

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Ripen, Produce Fruit, Bear Seed
s.d: to produce completely mature fruit
s.g: to produce ripe fruit; to bear mature fruit

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of τελευτάω ‘to end,’ not occurring in the NT) to come to the end of one’s life, as a euphemistic expression for death

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of τελευτή ‘end,’ not occurring in the NT) the end of one’s life, as a euphemistic expression for death
to bring an activity to a successful finish{N:001}
s.g: to complete; to finish; to end; to accomplish

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
s.d: (derivative of {L:τέλος<SDBG:τέλος:000000>}[a] ‘end,’ {D:67.66}) to occur or happen at the end of a duration
s.g: to end; to come to an end

s.d: to cause to happen for some end result
s.g: to make happen; to fulfill; to bring to fruition; to accomplish; fulfillment

s.d: to obey as a means of fulfilling the purpose of a rule or standard
s.c: The phrase ‘to obey the Law’ in ⟦Romans 2:27|Romans 2:27⟧ may be rendered simply as ‘to do what the Law says one must do.’

s.d: to pay tax or tribute (used absolutely or with a noun complement meaning ‘tax’ or ‘tribute’)
s.g: to pay taxes; to pay customs duty

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
s.d: a point of time marking the end of a duration
s.c: There are serious problems involved in rendering τέλος in ⟦Matthew 24:14|Matthew 24:14⟧ and in similar contexts. In a number of languages one simply cannot say ‘the end will come’; rather, it may be necessary to say ‘that is the finish’ or ‘everything is finished.’ In the context of ⟦Matthew 24:14|Matthew 24:14⟧, however, it may be best to translate ‘God will finish everything.’ The phrase εἰς τέλος in ⟦1 Thessalonians 2:16|1 Thessalonians 2:16⟧ may also be understood as an idiomatic expression involving a degree of completeness (see LN 78.47).

s.d: the result of an event or process, with special focus upon the final state or condition
s.c: In some languages τέλος in ⟦Matthew 26:58|Matthew 26:58⟧ may be rendered simply as ‘what would happen’ or ‘what would finally happen.’

s.d: the purpose of an event or state, viewed in terms of its result
a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result
s.c: It is also possible to understand the phrase ἕως τέλους in the temporal sense of ‘to the end’ (see LN 67.66).|It is also possible to understand τέλος in the expression εἰς τέλος in ⟦1 Thessalonians 2:16|1 Thessalonians 2:16⟧ as a temporal expression, with εἰς (LN 67.117) as a marker of an extent of time, so that this passage may be rendered as ‘and in the end wrath has come down on them’ or ‘and wrath has at last come down on them’ (see LN 67.66). In this context ὀργή may very well be translated as ‘punishment’ (LN 38.10), and in many languages it is necessary to indicate the agent of such punishment. The same ambiguity with εἰς τέλος occurs in ⟦John 13:1|John 13:1⟧ in the clause εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτούς, meaning ‘he loved them completely’ or ‘he loved them to the end’ (see LN 67.119).

s.d: payments customarily due a governmental authority
s.c: The term τέλος differs from κῆνσος (LN 57.180) in being somewhat more generic in meaning. In certain contexts τέλος may refer to various kinds of direct taxes, customs duties, and tribute money, but in contexts such as ⟦Matthew 17:25|Matthew 17:25⟧ in which κῆνσος also occurs, τέλος probably refers primarily to customs duties, while κῆνσος refers to a direct poll tax upon all adult males.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: the end) a marker of a conclusion to what has preceded, but not necessarily the conclusion of a text
(derivative of {L:τελέω<SDBG:τελέω:000004>}[e] ‘to pay taxes,’ {D:57.178}) one who collects taxes for the government
s.c: Since Jews who farmed the taxes for the Romans (that is to say, who paid Roman authorities for the privilege of collecting taxes) were considered traitors to their own people, the term τελώνης has strongly negative connotations in the NT. In any translation of the Gospels it may be especially important to have an adequate marginal note designed to explain the basis for the hostility which many people had toward tax collectors.

s.d: (derivative of {L:τελέω<SDBG:τελέω:000004>}[e] ‘to pay taxes,’ {D:57.178}) a place where taxes or revenue was collected from those entering a town to sell produce
s.c: In the ancient world taxes were primarily of two types: (1) a head tax on each individual (which was relatively small) and (2) revenue or tribute paid for goods and produce brought into an area for sale. The latter was essentially a kind of ‘sales tax,’ but paid by the seller who obviously increased the prices of goods accordingly.

s.d: an unusual sign, especially one in the heavens, serving to foretell impending events
s.c: In ancient times a portent might consist of a particular arrangement of the planets, an unusual display of northern lights, a conspicuous comet, or a cluster of falling stars. For a discussion of σημεῖον ‘sign,’ see LN 33.477.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person who sends greetings in {S:04501602200008}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an attorney who accused Paul before Felix
cardinal number, where there are four instances of a countable entity
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘from the four winds’ or ‘from the four directions’ is simply ‘from every direction.’ The Greek expression does not mean from only four specific directions, but rather from every direction.

s.d: fourteenth in a series involving either time, space, or set
cardinal number, where there are forty instances of a countable entity

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a very long period of time
s.c: Though most translations render ἔτη τεσσεράκοντα as ‘forty years,’ the expression probably is to be understood as meaning an unusually long period of time. See also discussion at LN 67.93.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (literally: forty days and forty nights) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
s.c: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (shortened form of [c] literally, forty days) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
s.c: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: pertaining to a period of forty years

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: pertaining to the fourth in a series of days
fourth in a series involving either time, space, or set
a fourth part of an object, series, or mass
s.c: For a discussion of some of the translational problems involved, see LN 60.63.

s.d: to function as a tetrarch (see {D:37.78})
s.g: to be a tetrarch; to be the governor of a region

s.d: a ruler with rank and authority lower than that of a king and one who ruled only with the approval of Roman authorities

s.dp: Features of Objects › Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Shapes
s.d: pertaining to having four equal sides and four right angles
a detachment of four soldiers
cardinal number, where there are four thousand instances of a countable entity
cardinal number, where there are four hundred instances of a countable entity

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: a period of four months{N:001}

s.dp: Number › Double, Four Times As Much, Etc. [Multiples]
s.d: four times as much in quantity
s.g: four times; four times as much

s.d: any four-footed animal, either wild or domesticated
s.c: A high percentage of languages appear to have no generic term to identify all kinds of quadrupeds whether wild or domesticated. Rather, they tend to make quite clear distinctions between wild and domesticated animals, and therefore it may be necessary to indicate both types in those contexts where the reference is to both wild as well as domesticated animals. For example, one may sometimes speak of ‘animals of the grass and animals of the forest’ or ‘animals of the barn and animals of the mountains.’|In ⟦Acts 10:12|Acts 10:12⟧ the reference is primarily to wild animals, since for the most part wild animals would be those designated as unclean. However, swine were also regarded as unclean, and they were domesticated.

s.d: (derivative of τέφρα ‘ashes,’ not occurring in the NT) to destroy by reducing something to ashes
s.c: It is possible to render ‘to reduce to ashes’ as ‘to burn up completely’ or ‘to destroy by fire and leave only ashes.’

s.d: an activity involving specialized training and skill
s.c: In a number of languages there is no special term for ‘craft,’ but an equivalent of this clause in ⟦Acts 18:3|Acts 18:3⟧ may be rendered as ‘for their work was making tents’ or ‘they earned money making tents’ or ‘they customarily made tents.’

s.d: one who customarily engages in a particular craft or occupation
to become liquid, either by melting or condensation
pertaining to a particularly clear or plain visual image
s.c: In ⟦Mark 8:25|Mark 8:25⟧ both διέβλεψεν (LN 24.35) and ἐνέβλεπεν (LN 24.9) occur. Some scholars assume that the two expressions are essentially equivalent in meaning, but others believe that διέβλεψεν is to be understood as ‘to look intently’ or ‘to focus one’s eyes upon.’

s.d: a reference to the size of something (occurring rarely in an absolute sense)

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: a degree which is comparable to some other expression of degree
s.g: so great; that great; so much
s.c: In a number of languages the closest equivalent of this expression in ⟦Revelation 16:18|Revelation 16:18⟧ may be ‘that earthquake was indeed very great.’

s.d: to cause a state to continue
s.g: to cause to continue; to retain; to keep
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 7:37|1 Corinthians 7:37⟧ the reference to ‘girl’ may be either a man’s daughter or a man’s fiancée. Because of the ambiguity of this statement in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:37|1 Corinthians 7:37⟧ and in view of the cultural complications involved, especially because of differences of customs in different parts of the world, it is important that translators add a note at this point explaining the difference of interpretation and some of the cultural implications.

s.d: to continue to hold in custody
s.g: to guard; to keep watch; custody
s.c: The act of holding someone in custody or guarding an individual may be expressed as ‘standing guard to see that someone will not escape’ or ‘watching carefully so that one cannot run off’ or ‘tying someone up so that he cannot leave.’

s.d: to continue to obey orders or commandments
s.g: to obey; to keep commandments; obedience

s.d: to continue to hold in custody
s.g: to guard; to keep watch; custody
s.c: The act of holding someone in custody or guarding an individual may be expressed as ‘standing guard to see that someone will not escape’ or ‘watching carefully so that one cannot run off’ or ‘tying someone up so that he cannot leave.’

s.d: a place of detention
s.c: Practically all languages have terms for a jail or a prison, though in some instances a descriptive phrase is employed, ‘a place where people are tied up’ or ‘a place to be chained.’ In some instances, highly idiomatic expressions are used, ‘a place for eating iron’ or ‘a room with rats.’

s.d: to continue to obey orders or commandments
s.g: to obey; to keep commandments; obedience

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city on the west shore of the Lake of Galilee

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the Lake of Tiberias, also known as the Lake of Galilee

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the Roman emperor Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus, who ruled from 14 A.D. to 37 A.D.; compare {D:93.214a}
to put or place in a particular location{N:001}

s.dp: Control, Rule › Assign to a Role or Function
s.d: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
s.g: to appoint; to designate; to assign; to give a task to

s.d: to remove or take off clothing
to explain something, presumably by putting forward additional or different information

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Lend, Loan, Interest, Borrow, Bank
s.d: to deposit money with a banker, with the intent of earning interest
s.g: to deposit; to put in a bank

s.d: to cause a state to be{N:003}
s.g: to cause to be; to make to be; to make; to result in; to bring upon; to bring about

s.d: to cause someone to experience, with the implication of subjecting a person to something
s.g: to make experience; to subject to

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to put a plan) to suggest a plan of action
(an idiom, literally: to put into the ears) to listen carefully to, with the implication of not forgetting
s.c: For another interpretation of this idiom in ⟦Luke 9:44|Luke 9:44⟧, see LN 29.5.

s.dp: Memory and Recall › Storing of Information
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to place in the ears) to continue to bear something in mind
s.g: to bear in mind; to remember well; to not forget
s.c: For another interpretation of the idiom τίθεμαι εἰς τὰ ὦτα in ⟦Luke 9:44|Luke 9:44⟧, see LN 24.64.

s.dp: Memory and Recall › Storing of Information
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to place in the heart) to store information in the mind, with the implication of its being valuable
s.g: to treasure up in the heart; to store in the mind as valuable

s.d: (idioms, literally: to place in the heart, and: to place in the mind) to engage in the process of deciding
s.g: to make up one’s mind; to decide
s.c: It is also possible to interpret the phrase ἐν τῷ πνεύματι in ⟦Acts 19:21|Acts 19:21⟧ as being a reference to the Holy Spirit and accordingly, the passage may be translated as ‘Paul, led by the Spirit, decided to travel through Macedonia.’

s.d: (idioms, literally: to put at someone’s feet) to present something to someone who is reckoned as having superior status or position
s.g: to turn over to; to put at someone’s disposal

s.dp: Stances and Events Related to Stances › Kneel
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to place the knees, a Latinism) to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
s.c: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to lay down one’s life) to die, with the implication of voluntary or willing action
s.g: to die voluntarily; to die willingly
s.c: Though in English the phrases ‘to lay down one’s life’ or ‘to give one’s life’ do suggest a voluntary dying, a literal rendering of such expressions in other languages would not necessarily imply the same. It may therefore be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to die willingly’ or ‘to die without resisting.’ In some languages ‘willingly’ is expressed primarily as a negation of objecting, for example, ‘I will not object to dying.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: to give birth to a child{N:001}
s.c: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Grow, Growth
s.d: to cause the growth and production of plants
to pluck or pick by pulling off or out of

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the father of Bartimaeus

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: to attribute high status to someone by honoring

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Pay, Price, Cost
s.d: to determine an amount to be used in paying for something
s.g: to set a price on; to determine the cost
s.c: It would also be possible to translate ‘the price set on him by the people of Israel’ as ‘the amount the people of Israel had agreed to pay for him.’

s.d: to provide aid or financial assistance, with the implication that this is an appropriate means of showing respect
s.g: to give assistance to; to provide for the needs of as a sign of respect; to support and honor

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: honor as an element in the assignment of status to a person
the worth or merit of some object, event, or state
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘value’ is almost always in terms of ‘importance.’ This is particularly true if one is speaking of objects which are normally not bought and sold. Accordingly, one may render this particular expression in ⟦1 Corinthians 12:23|1 Corinthians 12:23⟧ as ‘those parts of the body which we think of as not being so important, to these we grant particular importance’ or ‘… we consider as being very important.’|It is also possible to interpret τιμή in ⟦1 Corinthians 12:23|1 Corinthians 12:23⟧ as a degree of honor or appreciation (see τιμή, LN 87.4).

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Pay, Price, Cost
s.d: the amount of money or property regarded as representing the value or price of something
s.c: It would be wrong to assume that τιμή in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:23|1 Corinthians 7:23⟧ necessarily means ‘a high price.’ The notion ‘high’ comes from the contextual reference to the death of Christ. In ⟦1 Corinthians 7:23|1 Corinthians 7:23⟧, however, the implication is that a price was set and that the payment has been made. If the passive expression in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:23|1 Corinthians 7:23⟧ must be made active, one may translate as ‘Christ bought you with a price’ or ‘Christ paid for you.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Pay, Price, Cost
s.d: compensation given for special service, with the implication that this is a way by which honor or respect may be shown
s.c: τιμή in the sense of compensation is related in meaning to τιμάω to support, to provide for (LN 57.117) and τιμή cost (LN 57.161), but in ⟦1 Timothy 5:17|1 Timothy 5:17⟧ it is also possible to understand τιμή in the sense of τιμή honor, respect (LN 87.4), and therefore one may speak of the elders as receiving double honor.

s.d: pertaining to being of considerable value or worth
s.c: It is possible to interpret λίθους τιμίους in ⟦1 Corinthians 3:12|1 Corinthians 3:12⟧ as a unit which means ‘precious stones’ (see LN 2.29), but in this figurative context of a foundation, the reference may very well be more general.

s.dp: Status › Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
s.d: pertaining to high status, involving both honor and respect

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Be Rich, Be Wealthy
s.d: (derivative of {L:τίμιος<SDBG:τίμιος:000000>}[a] ‘valuable, precious,’ {D:65.2}) a large quantity of costly, valuable possessions
s.c: ‘Wealth’ may usually be rendered by ‘the many valuable possessions.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a friend and coworker of Paul

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: one of the seven helpers in the church in Jerusalem
to punish, with the implication of causing people to suffer what they deserve
s.g: to punish; to suffer punishment (with passive construction); punishment

s.d: to punish, with the implication of causing people to suffer what they deserve
s.g: to punish; to suffer punishment (with passive construction); punishment

s.d: to experience something bad, often in retribution for some wrongdoing
